last_observation.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+3z=-2 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2y-3z-2 \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ and $z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y-3z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y+12z=-8 \\ x-2y+3z=-2 \\ -2x+4y-6z=4\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

Question 20

Consider the following system of linear equations: {4x−8y+12z=−8x−2y+3z=−2−2x+4y−6z=4 Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix M of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

a
[2y+3z+2yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
b
No solution
c
[y−2z−1yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
d
[2−2y+3zyz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
e
[2y−3z−2yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The augmented matrix for this system is M=[4−812−81−23−2−24−64].

Transforming M to reduced row echelon form, we have

M∼[4−812−81−23−2−24−64]R1↔R2∼[1−23−24−812−8−24−64]R2:=R2−4R1∼[1−23−20000−24−64]R3:=R3+2R1∼[1−23−200000000].

The corresponding system is now {x−2y+3z=−20x+0y+0z=00x+0y+0z=0.

Since any numbers x,y,z form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system.

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have two free variables, y, and z. That means we need to find x in terms of y and z.

Therefore, the general solution is

{x=2y−3z−2y=yz=z,

where y and z (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as [xyz]=[2y−3z−2yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Reduced Row Echelon Form of a Singular 3x3 System With One Pivot

solution.reasoning: Divide R_1 by 4 to obtain [1,−2,3 | −2]. Then R_2←R_2−R_1 and R_3←R_3+2R_1 produce two zero rows. Thus x−2y+3z=−2, giving x=2y−3z−2 with y and z arbitrary, matching choice e. No MA answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different system.

feedback.name: Question 20
feedback.problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y+12z=-8 \\ x-2y+3z=-2 \\ -2x+4y-6z=4\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
feedback.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ to reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 12 & -8 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & -6 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+3z=-2 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2y-3z-2 \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ and $z$ (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2y-3z-2 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}

feedback.html:
Question 20
?

Consider the following system of linear equations: {4x−8y+12z=−8x−2y+3z=−2−2x+4y−6z=4 Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix M of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

a
[2y+3z+2yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
b
No solution
c
[y−2z−1yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
d
[2−2y+3zyz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
e
[2y−3z−2yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The augmented matrix for this system is M=[4−812−81−23−2−24−64].

Transforming M to reduced row echelon form, we have

M∼[4−812−81−23−2−24−64]R1↔R2∼[1−23−24−812−8−24−64]R2:=R2−4R1∼[1−23−20000−24−64]R3:=R3+2R1∼[1−23−200000000].

The corresponding system is now {x−2y+3z=−20x+0y+0z=00x+0y+0z=0.

Since any numbers x,y,z form a solution of the final two equations, we can remove these equations from the system.

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have two free variables, y, and z. That means we need to find x in terms of y and z.

Therefore, the general solution is

{x=2y−3z−2y=yz=z,

where y and z (the free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as [xyz]=[2y−3z−2yz],y,z∈(−∞,∞).

$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[0,2]$ and $[1,2]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-0=2, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
5{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=5\cdot 2\cdot 1=10.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,2]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,2]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}2Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}2Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that both ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are equal to the length of the interval $[1,2].$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-1=1, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Combining our results, we have 

$$
2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=2\cdot 1\cdot 1=2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following partitions:

- $P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[-1, 2]$

- $P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2, 3]$

Calculate $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n {3} \Delta x_i \Delta y_j,$ where $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}$ and $\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\Delta x_i$ and $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[-1, 2]$ and $[2,3]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-(-1)=3, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
3 \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 = 9.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:

tutorials.name: Calculating a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition
tutorials.problem:
We have our partition $P = P_1\times P_2,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14248952/assets/0e497b6d43e4d46d4fad71bc2b81810c972b0e306817d161ad3a2e285e6b9d6e.png)

Let $\Delta x_i$ be the difference in the $x$-values of any two successive points in $P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}
$$

Similarly, let $\Delta y_j$ be the difference in the $y$-values of any two successive points in $P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}
$$

It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j
$$

Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

- Here, the $x_i$'s partition the interval $[1,4]$ which has length $4 - 1 = 3.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.$

- Similarly, the $y_j$'s partition the interval $[2,4]$ which has length $4 - 2 = 2.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3$ represents the width of the rectangle, while $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2$ represents the height.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j$ represents the area of the rectangle.

tutorial.name: Calculating a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition
tutorial.problem:
We have our partition $P = P_1\times P_2,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14248952/assets/0e497b6d43e4d46d4fad71bc2b81810c972b0e306817d161ad3a2e285e6b9d6e.png)

Let $\Delta x_i$ be the difference in the $x$-values of any two successive points in $P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}
$$

Similarly, let $\Delta y_j$ be the difference in the $y$-values of any two successive points in $P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}
$$

It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j
$$

Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

- Here, the $x_i$'s partition the interval $[1,4]$ which has length $4 - 1 = 3.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.$

- Similarly, the $y_j$'s partition the interval $[2,4]$ which has length $4 - 2 = 2.$ So, we have $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}\cdot {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3$ represents the width of the rectangle, while $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2$ represents the height.

- $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j$ represents the area of the rectangle.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}3Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =3{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\Delta x_i$ and $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[-1, 2]$ and $[2,3]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-(-1)=3, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
3 \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 = 9.
$$

$$

$$

Combining our results, we have

$$

Question 7
?

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [2,5]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [0,3]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)ΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
18
b
30
c
27
d
19
e
15
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

∑i=1mΔxi⋅∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)Δyj.

Note that ∑i=1mΔxi is just the length of the interval [2,5]. So, we have

∑i=1mΔxi=5−2=3.

For the sum over j, we evaluate it as follows:

∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)Δyj=(y1+y0)Δy1+(y2+y1)Δy2+⋯+(yn+xn−1)Δyn=(y1+y0)(y1−y0)+(y2+y1)(y2−y1)+⋯+(yn+xn−1)(yn−yn−1)=(y12−y02)+(y22−y12)+⋯+(yn2−yn−12)=(y12−y02)+(y22−y12)+⋯+(yn2−yn−12)=−y02+yn2=yn2−y02=32−02=9

Combining our results, we finally arrive at

∑i=1mΔxi⋅∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)Δyj=3⋅9=27.

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [0,2]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [1,2]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1n2(xi+xi−1)ΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
8
b
4
c
2
d
1
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

2∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj.

Note that ∑j=1nΔyj is just the length of the interval [1,2]. So, we have

∑j=1nΔyj=2−1=1.

For the sum over i, we evaluate it as follows:

∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi=(x1+x0)Δx1+(x2+x1)Δx2+⋯+(xm+xm−1)Δxn=(x1+x0)(x1−x0)+(x2+x1)(x2−x1)+⋯+(xm+xm−1)(xm−xm−1)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=−x02+xm2=xm2−x02=22−02=4

Combining our results, we finally arrive at

2∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj=2⋅4⋅1=8.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[0,2]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,2]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}5Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}5Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =5{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =5{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[0,2]$ and $[1,2]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-0=2, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
5{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=5\cdot 2\cdot 1=10.
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition
last_observation.worked_solution:
Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[1,5]$ and $[5,7]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =5-1=4, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =7-5=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=4\cdot 2=8.
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [1,5]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [5,7]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1nΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
10
b
8
c
9
d
6
e
12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

∑i=1m∑j=1nΔxiΔyj=∑i=1mΔxi∑j=1nΔyj.

Note that ∑i=1mΔxi and ∑j=1nΔyj are just the lengths of the intervals [1,5] and [5,7] respectively. So, we have

∑i=1mΔxi=5−1=4,∑j=1nΔyj=7−5=2.

Combining our results, we have

∑i=1mΔxi∑j=1nΔyj=4⋅2=8.

solution.reasoning: The double sum factors as (\sum_i\Delta x_i)(\sum_j\Delta y_j). Each sum telescopes to its interval length, giving (5-1)(7-5)=4\cdot2=8, option b. The supplied example demonstrates the method but provides no Math Academy answer evidence for this current question.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[0,4]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[2,8]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are just the lengths of the intervals $[0,4]$ and $[2,8]$ respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =4-0=4, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =8-2=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=4\cdot 6=24.
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the following partitions:

- ${P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,2]$

- ${P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is a partition of the interval $[1,2]$

Calculate ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}2Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j},$ where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}2Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that both ${\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}$ and ${\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}$ are equal to the length of the interval $[1,2].$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =2-1=1, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Combining our results, we have 

$$
2{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=2\cdot 1\cdot 1=2.
$$

question.problem:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i} & =3-1=2, \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j} & =6-3=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining our results, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}Δ{x}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{y}_{j}=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [−3,−1]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [−2,1]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1n−2(xi+xi−1)ΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
48
b
−24
c
56
d
−42
e
36
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

−2∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj.

Note that ∑j=1nΔyj is just the length of the interval [−2,1]. So, we have

∑j=1nΔyj=1−(−2)=3.

For the sum over i, we evaluate it as follows:

∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi=(x1+x0)Δx1+(x2+x1)Δx2+⋯+(xm+xm−1)Δxn=(x1+x0)(x1−x0)+(x2+x1)(x2−x1)+⋯+(xm+xm−1)(xm−xm−1)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=−x02+xm2=xm2−x02=(−1)2−(−3)2=−8

Combining our results, we finally arrive at −2∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj=(−2)⋅(−8)⋅3=48.

question.problem:

question.html:
Question 7
?

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [2,5]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [0,3]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)ΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
18
b
30
c
27
d
19
e
15
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

∑i=1mΔxi⋅∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)Δyj.

Note that ∑i=1mΔxi is just the length of the interval [2,5]. So, we have

∑i=1mΔxi=5−2=3.

For the sum over j, we evaluate it as follows:

∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)Δyj=(y1+y0)Δy1+(y2+y1)Δy2+⋯+(yn+xn−1)Δyn=(y1+y0)(y1−y0)+(y2+y1)(y2−y1)+⋯+(yn+xn−1)(yn−yn−1)=(y12−y02)+(y22−y12)+⋯+(yn2−yn−12)=(y12−y02)+(y22−y12)+⋯+(yn2−yn−12)=−y02+yn2=yn2−y02=32−02=9

Combining our results, we finally arrive at

∑i=1mΔxi⋅∑j=1n(yj+yj−1)Δyj=3⋅9=27.
question.knowledge_point: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares

solution.reasoning: Factor the sum into (\sum_i\Delta x_i)(\sum_j(y_j+y_{j-1})\Delta y_j). The first factor is 5-2=3. Since (y_j+y_{j-1})(y_j-y_{j-1})=y_j^2-y_{j-1}^2, the second telescopes to 3^2-0^2=9. Thus the answer is 27, option c. No Math Academy answer evidence for this current question is supplied.

question.html:
Question 8
?

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [0,2]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [1,2]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1n2(xi+xi−1)ΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
8
b
4
c
2
d
1
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

2∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj.

Note that ∑j=1nΔyj is just the length of the interval [1,2]. So, we have

∑j=1nΔyj=2−1=1.

For the sum over i, we evaluate it as follows:

∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi=(x1+x0)Δx1+(x2+x1)Δx2+⋯+(xm+xm−1)Δxn=(x1+x0)(x1−x0)+(x2+x1)(x2−x1)+⋯+(xm+xm−1)(xm−xm−1)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=−x02+xm2=xm2−x02=22−02=4

Combining our results, we finally arrive at

2∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj=2⋅4⋅1=8.

question.html:
Question 10
?

Consider the following partitions:

  • P1={x0,x1,…,xm} is a partition of the interval [1,3]

  • P2={y0,y1,…,yn} is a partition of the interval [−2,0]

Calculate ∑i=1m∑j=1n7(xi+xi−1)ΔxiΔyj, where Δxi=xi−xi−1 and Δyj=yj−yj−1.

a
119
b
112
c
105
d
98
e
116
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

7∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj.

Note that ∑j=1nΔyj is just the length of the interval [−2,0]. So, we have

∑j=1nΔyj=0−(−2)=2.

For the sum over i, we evaluate it as follows:

∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi=(x1+x0)Δx1+(x2+x1)Δx2+⋯+(xm+xm−1)Δxn=(x1+x0)(x1−x0)+(x2+x1)(x2−x1)+⋯+(xm+xm−1)(xm−xm−1)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=(x12−x02)+(x22−x12)+⋯+(xm2−xm−12)=−x02+xm2=xm2−x02=32−12=8

Combining our results, we finally arrive at 7∑i=1m(xi+xi−1)Δxi⋅∑j=1nΔyj=7⋅8⋅2=112.

question.knowledge_point: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares

solution.reasoning: The identity (x_i+x_{i-1})\Delta x_i=x_i^2-x_{i-1}^2 makes the x-sum telescope to 3^2-1^2=8. The y-widths sum to 0-(-2)=2. Therefore the double sum equals 7\cdot8\cdot2=112, option b. The supplied example does not establish Math Academy's answer for this current question.

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/0cb01fa25e07a0f18655c9b61b732ca0738ea6fbe735422f92925a7dcc6963be.png)

What is the total surface area of the rectangular prism represented by the net above?
questions.worked_solution:
The surface area of our prism consists of $2$ squares (base and top) and $4$ rectangles (side faces). 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =2\times (\text{Area of the base})+4\times (\text{Area of the side}) \\  & =2\times 9+4\times 12 \\  & =18+48 \\  & =66\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/4ae8d09f2e4bca084d113aaa06f80570da8d628868ccd3c9c208337de303d068.png)

What is the total surface area of the triangular prism represented by the net above?
questions.worked_solution:
The surface area of our prism consists of $2$ triangles (base and top) and $3$ rectangles (side faces). 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =2\times (\text{Area of the base})+3\times (\text{Area of the side}) \\  & =2\times 8+3\times 30 \\  & =16+90 \\  & =106\,{\text{mm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Liz deconstructs a lantern and gets the net shown above. In the figure, the areas of two of its faces are shown. What is the total surface area of the lantern?
questions.worked_solution:
The net shown corresponds to a triangular pyramid. The surface area of our pyramid consists of $1$ triangle (base) and $3$ triangles (side faces). 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =1\times (\text{Area of the base})+3\times (\text{Area of the side}) \\  & =1\times 5+3\times 13 \\  & =5+39 \\  & =44\,{\text{in}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

A manufacturer produces an unfair tetrahedral die from a plastic net, shown above. What is the total surface area of the die?
questions.worked_solution:
The net shown corresponds to a triangular pyramid. The surface area of our pyramid consists of $1$ base triangle and $3$ side triangles. 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =1\times (\text{Area of base})+3\times (\text{Area of side}) \\  & =1\times 64+3\times 78 \\  & =64+234 \\  & =298\,{\text{mm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/248ccfcbb3de8ab63622cfaf4c823ae1c1734742f5f8c9f14b1dfae0ff79eed2.png)

What is the surface area of the box shown above knowing that  it is $4\,\text{m}$ long, $1\,\text{m}$ wide, and $1\,\text{m}$ tall?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the net of our box.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/c35bb0f7b049baa569a06532b516436afaf310e28870cfbd4790467d36e54809.png)

$$

$$

 

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are $4\,\text{m}$ long and $1\,\text{m}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is:

$$
\text{Area of the rectangle}=4\times 1=4\,{\text{m}}^{2}.
$$

The squares has the side equal to $1\,\text{m}.$ Hence, the area of one square is:

$$
\text{Area of the square}=1\times 1=1\,{\text{m}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the box consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares. 

Therefore, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of the rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of the square}) \\  & =4\times 4+2\times 1 \\  & =16+2 \\  & =18\,{\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/72450d407a3c4d043769ac1e331adc1625fd8d579e5f49409cfa718116e05581.png)

Nash paints a box that has the form of a rectangular prism. What is the total area that Nash needs to paint if the box is $6\,\text{cm}$ long, $3\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $3\,\text{cm}$ tall?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the net of our box.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/038c0ea6632481ee1eaece1637aac46b9a09389c0d363f4b3503b1944c039127.png)

$$

$$

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are $6\,\text{cm}$ long and $3\,\text{cm}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is

$$
\text{Area of the rectangle}=6\times 3=18\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

The squares have sides of length $3\,\text{cm}.$ Hence, the area of one square is

$$
\text{Area of the square}=3\times 3=9\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the bar consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares. 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of the rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of the square}) \\  & =4\times 18+2\times 9 \\  & =72+18 \\  & =90\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The net of our pyramid is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/c4a5fe995aaaf47b7ab2b90492059d739fc2352955dc1e12a71852fc13046a33.png)

$$
\text{Area of square} = 5 \times 5 = 25 \, \text{in}^2.
$$

 

Each side face of our solid is triangle, where the base is $5\,\text{in}$ and the height is $8\,\text{in}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\text{Area of triangle} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 8 = 20 \, \text{in}^2.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the pyramid consists of $1$ square (the base) and $4$ triangles (the side faces). 

Adding the areas, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =1\times (\text{Area of the square})+4\times (\text{Area of the triangle}) \\  & =1\times 25+4\times 20 \\  & =25+80 \\  & =105\,{\text{in}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
If we know a polyhedron's measurements, we can calculate its surface area by first drawing the net of the polyhedron. Then, we calculate the areas of its polygonal faces using known formulas and then sum the results. 

To demonstrate, let's find the surface area of the rectangular prism shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/85ddfbae506653a6b2c4982be74f9eff2b91df55a5075597ddbbd42a51cc2f52.png)

 

First, we consider the net of our prism.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/9874d746b2510403accdbd2e9d77ce8d5bc917b76e68c3f1690a24e8643ad473.png)

      

From the diagram, we see that the prism is made up of squares and rectangles.

- The rectangles are $8\,\text{ft}$ long and $2\,\text{ft}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is

$$
\text{Area of rectangle} = 8 \times 2 = 16 \, \text{ft}^2.
$$

- The squares have sides of length $2\, \text{ft}.$ So, the area of one square is

$$
\text{Area of square} = 2 \times 2 = 4 \, \text{ft}^2.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the prism consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares.

Adding the areas, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of square}) \\  & =4\times 16+2\times 4 \\  & =64+8 \\  & =72\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.problem:
If we know a polyhedron's measurements, we can calculate its surface area by first drawing the net of the polyhedron. Then, we calculate the areas of its polygonal faces using known formulas and then sum the results. 

To demonstrate, let's find the surface area of the rectangular prism shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/85ddfbae506653a6b2c4982be74f9eff2b91df55a5075597ddbbd42a51cc2f52.png)

 

First, we consider the net of our prism.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/9874d746b2510403accdbd2e9d77ce8d5bc917b76e68c3f1690a24e8643ad473.png)

      

From the diagram, we see that the prism is made up of squares and rectangles.

- The rectangles are $8\,\text{ft}$ long and $2\,\text{ft}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is

$$
\text{Area of rectangle} = 8 \times 2 = 16 \, \text{ft}^2.
$$

- The squares have sides of length $2\, \text{ft}.$ So, the area of one square is

$$
\text{Area of square} = 2 \times 2 = 4 \, \text{ft}^2.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the prism consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares.

Adding the areas, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of square}) \\  & =4\times 16+2\times 4 \\  & =64+8 \\  & =72\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that the base of the pyramid is a square with sides equal to $5 \, \text{in}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\text{Area of square} = 5 \times 5 = 25 \, \text{in}^2.
$$

 

Each side face of our solid is triangle, where the base is $5\,\text{in}$ and the height is $8\,\text{in}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\text{Area of triangle} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 8 = 20 \, \text{in}^2.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the pyramid consists of $1$ square (the base) and $4$ triangles (the side faces). 

Adding the areas, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =1\times (\text{Area of the square})+4\times (\text{Area of the triangle}) \\  & =1\times 25+4\times 20 \\  & =25+80 \\  & =105\,{\text{in}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

18cm2
c

The surface area of our prism consists of 2 squares (base and top) and 4 rectangles (side faces).

Surface area=2×(Area of the base)+4×(Area of the side)=2×9+4×12=18+48=66cm2.

feedback.html:
Question 1
?

What is the total surface area of the rectangular prism represented by the net above?

a
66cm2
b
18cm2
c
48cm2
d
62cm2
e
72cm2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The surface area of our prism consists of 2 squares (base and top) and 4 rectangles (side faces).

Therefore, we get

Surface area=2×(Area of the base)+4×(Area of the side)=2×9+4×12=18+48=66cm2.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/4ae8d09f2e4bca084d113aaa06f80570da8d628868ccd3c9c208337de303d068.png)

What is the total surface area of the triangular prism represented by the net above?
question.worked_solution:
The surface area of our prism consists of $2$ triangles (base and top) and $3$ rectangles (side faces). 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =2\times (\text{Area of the base})+3\times (\text{Area of the side}) \\  & =2\times 8+3\times 30 \\  & =16+90 \\  & =106\,{\text{mm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

What is the total surface area of the triangular prism represented by the net above?

a
16mm2
b
106mm2
c
90mm2
d
116mm2
e
100mm2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The surface area of our prism consists of 2 triangles (base and top) and 3 rectangles (side faces).

Therefore, we get

Surface area=2×(Area of the base)+3×(Area of the side)=2×8+3×30=16+90=106mm2.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Surface Area of a Polyhedron Given the Areas of the Faces

solution.reasoning: The net depicts two congruent triangles of area 8 mm² each and three congruent rectangles of area 30 mm² each. Total surface area is 2(8)+3(30)=106 mm², option b. No answer or grade from Math Academy is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different prism.

Liz deconstructs a lantern and gets the net shown above. In the figure, the areas of two of its faces are shown. What is the total surface area of the lantern?
question.worked_solution:
The net shown corresponds to a triangular pyramid. The surface area of our pyramid consists of $1$ triangle (base) and $3$ triangles (side faces). 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =1\times (\text{Area of the base})+3\times (\text{Area of the side}) \\  & =1\times 5+3\times 13 \\  & =5+39 \\  & =44\,{\text{in}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

A manufacturer produces an unfair tetrahedral die from a plastic net, shown above. What is the total surface area of the die?

a
302mm2
b
274mm2
c
264mm2
d
298mm2
e
286mm2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The net shown corresponds to a triangular pyramid. The surface area of our pyramid consists of 1 base triangle and 3 side triangles.

Therefore, we get

Surface area=1×(Area of base)+3×(Area of side)=1×64+3×78=64+234=298mm2.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/248ccfcbb3de8ab63622cfaf4c823ae1c1734742f5f8c9f14b1dfae0ff79eed2.png)

What is the surface area of the box shown above knowing that  it is $4\,\text{m}$ long, $1\,\text{m}$ wide, and $1\,\text{m}$ tall?
question.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the net of our box.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/c35bb0f7b049baa569a06532b516436afaf310e28870cfbd4790467d36e54809.png)

$$

$$

 

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are $4\,\text{m}$ long and $1\,\text{m}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is:

$$
\text{Area of the rectangle}=4\times 1=4\,{\text{m}}^{2}.
$$

The squares has the side equal to $1\,\text{m}.$ Hence, the area of one square is:

$$
\text{Area of the square}=1\times 1=1\,{\text{m}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the box consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares. 

Therefore, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of the rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of the square}) \\  & =4\times 4+2\times 1 \\  & =16+2 \\  & =18\,{\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}

Question 5
?

What is the surface area of the box shown above knowing that it is 4m long, 1m wide, and 1m tall?

a
18m2
b
16m2
c
24m2
d
12m2
e
15m2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's consider the net of our box.


From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are 4m long and 1m high. So, the area of one rectangle is: Area of the rectangle=4×1=4m2.

The squares has the side equal to 1m. Hence, the area of one square is: Area of the square=1×1=1m2.

Finally, the surface area of the box consists of 4 rectangles and 2 squares.

Therefore, we get:

Surface area=4×(Area of the rectangle)+2×(Area of the square)=4×4+2×1=16+2=18m2.

Question 5
?

What is the surface area of the box shown above knowing that it is 4m long, 1m wide, and 1m tall?

a
18m2
b
16m2
c
24m2
d
12m2
e
15m2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's consider the net of our box.


From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are 4m long and 1m high. So, the area of one rectangle is: Area of the rectangle=4×1=4m2.

The squares has the side equal to 1m. Hence, the area of one square is: Area of the square=1×1=1m2.

Finally, the surface area of the box consists of 4 rectangles and 2 squares.

Therefore, we get:

Surface area=4×(Area of the rectangle)+2×(Area of the square)=4×4+2×1=16+2=18m2.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/72450d407a3c4d043769ac1e331adc1625fd8d579e5f49409cfa718116e05581.png)

Nash paints a box that has the form of a rectangular prism. What is the total area that Nash needs to paint if the box is $6\,\text{cm}$ long, $3\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $3\,\text{cm}$ tall?
question.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the net of our box.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/038c0ea6632481ee1eaece1637aac46b9a09389c0d363f4b3503b1944c039127.png)

$$

$$

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are $6\,\text{cm}$ long and $3\,\text{cm}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is

$$
\text{Area of the rectangle}=6\times 3=18\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

The squares have sides of length $3\,\text{cm}.$ Hence, the area of one square is

$$
\text{Area of the square}=3\times 3=9\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the bar consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares. 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of the rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of the square}) \\  & =4\times 18+2\times 9 \\  & =72+18 \\  & =90\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Nash paints a box that has the form of a rectangular prism. What is the total area that Nash needs to paint if the box is 6cm long, 3cm wide, and 3cm tall?

a
90cm2
b
108cm2
c
72cm2
d
86cm2
e
54cm2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's consider the net of our box.

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are 6cm long and 3cm high. So, the area of one rectangle is Area of the rectangle=6×3=18cm2.

The squares have sides of length 3cm. Hence, the area of one square is Area of the square=3×3=9cm2.

Finally, the surface area of the bar consists of 4 rectangles and 2 squares.

Therefore, we get

Surface area=4×(Area of the rectangle)+2×(Area of the square)=4×18+2×9=72+18=90cm2.

solution.reasoning: The total painted area is the surface area of all six faces: 2(lw+lh+wh)=2(6×3+6×3+3×3)=90 cm², option a. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different solid.

feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the net of our box.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249141/assets/038c0ea6632481ee1eaece1637aac46b9a09389c0d363f4b3503b1944c039127.png)

$$

$$

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are $6\,\text{cm}$ long and $3\,\text{cm}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is

$$
\text{Area of the rectangle}=6\times 3=18\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

The squares have sides of length $3\,\text{cm}.$ Hence, the area of one square is

$$
\text{Area of the square}=3\times 3=9\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the bar consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares. 

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of the rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of the square}) \\  & =4\times 18+2\times 9 \\  & =72+18 \\  & =90\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x-2} & ={5}^{4x} \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x-2}) & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
x-2={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{4x}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x-2=4x{log}_{3}⁡(5)
$$

Then, we solve for $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x & =2+4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =2 \\ x(1-4{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-4{log}_{3}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(5)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}≈1.464\,974.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2}{1-4(1.464\,974)}≈-0.412,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that ${3}^{x}={2}^{x-1},$ what is the value of $x?$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x} & ={2}^{x-1} \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x}) & ={log}_{3}⁡({2}^{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡({2}^{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(x-1){log}_{3}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(x-1){log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x & =x{log}_{3}⁡(2)-{log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(2) & =-{log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(2)) & =-{log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x & =-\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(2)}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(2)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}≈0.630\,930.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈-\frac{0.630\,930}{1-0.630\,930}≈-1.710,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x-5}={4}^{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-5} & ={4}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & =5 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x-1}={3}^{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-1} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & ={2}^{x+3} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x+3}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+2=(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x+2 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2 \\ x & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{x+4}={6}^{2-3x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+4} & ={6}^{2-3x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2-3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{2x}={8}^{1-6x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2x} & ={8}^{1-6x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{1-6x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8))}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{4-x} & ={8}^{2x+3} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{4-x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{2x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(4-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)=(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ -x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x & =\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
canonical_examples.problem: Expressed in terms of $\log_2,$ what value of $x$ satisfies the equation $2^{x+1}=3^x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take $\log_2$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x} \\ {log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x+1}) & ={log}_{2}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 = \log_2 \left(3^{x}\right)
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+1 = x \log_2 \left(3\right)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ x{log}_{2}⁡(3)-x & =1 \\ x({log}_{2}⁡(3)-1) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{2}⁡(3)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
canonical_examples.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation $e^{x+1}=2^x\cdot 5?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+1} & ={2}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\ln \left( e^a \right) = a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 =\ln \left(2^{x}\cdot 5\right)
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, determine the value of $x$ that satisfies the equation $5^{x+2}=9^{x-2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+2} & ={9}^{x-2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x-2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(x+2)\ln(5) = (x-2)\ln(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\ x & =\frac{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9))}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The most general way of solving exponential equations with different bases is to use logarithms on both sides of the equation. 
For example, given the equation

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}⁡(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}⁡(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x-2} & ={5}^{4x} \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x-2}) & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
x-2={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{4x}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x-2=4x{log}_{3}⁡(5)
$$

Then, we solve for $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x & =2+4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =2 \\ x(1-4{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-4{log}_{3}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(5)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}≈1.464\,974.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2}{1-4(1.464\,974)}≈-0.412,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+1} & ={2}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\ln \left( e^a \right) = a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 =\ln \left(2^{x}\cdot 5\right)
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex−5=4x?

a
5(1−ln⁡4)
b
51−ln⁡4
c
5ln⁡4
d
1+ln⁡45
e
ln⁡5−ln⁡4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−5=4xln⁡(ex−5)=ln⁡(4x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x−5=ln⁡(4x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−5=xln⁡4

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x−5=xln⁡4x−xln⁡4=5x(1−ln⁡4)=5x=51−ln⁡4

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-1} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-1} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

a
1−ln⁡3
b
11−ln⁡3
c
1−ln⁡33
d
ln⁡2−ln⁡3
e
log⁡31+ln⁡3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−1=3xln⁡(ex−1)=ln⁡(3x)

x−1=ln⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−1=xln⁡3

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & ={2}^{x+3} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x+3}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+2=(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x+2 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2 \\ x & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+2} & ={9}^{x-2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x-2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(x+2)\ln(5) = (x-2)\ln(9).
$$

$$

$$

question.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, determine the value of $x$ that satisfies the equation $5^{x+2}=9^{x-2}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+2} & ={9}^{x-2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x-2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(x+2)\ln(5) = (x-2)\ln(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\ x & =\frac{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9))}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(4-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)=(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8).

$$
\begin{aligned}(4-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ -x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x & =\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}\end{aligned}

judgments.reasoning: Taking logarithms gives x=2\ln 3/(\ln 3-4\ln 5)≈-0.411532, which rounds to -0.412. The earlier answer was correct: Math Academy graded the submitted -0.412 Correct, and its worked solution agrees.

Taking logarithms yields x=-\ln 2/(\ln 3-\ln 2)≈-1.709511, which rounds to -1.710, option e. This agrees with the earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

Taking logarithms gives x-5=x\ln 4, hence x=5/(1-\ln 4), option b, agreeing with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The actual submitted response was option a, 5(1-\ln 4), which was correctly graded Incorrect; that grade does not contradict option b.
Taking natural logarithms gives x-1=x\ln 3, hence x=1/(1-\ln 3), option b. This matches my earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

Taking logarithms gives x+2=(x+3)\ln 2, hence x=(3\ln 2-2)/(1-\ln 2). My earlier answer and the submitted response match this result and were graded Correct. Math Academy's worked solution is identical apart from logarithm notation and parentheses.

Taking logarithms gives (x+4)\ln 3=(2-3x)\ln 6, so x=(2\ln 6-4\ln 3)/(\ln 3+3\ln 6), option a. This matches my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The actual submission was option b, correctly graded Incorrect; that grade does not contradict option a.
Taking logarithms gives 2x\ln 3=(1-6x)\ln 8, hence x=\ln 8/[2(\ln 3+3\ln 8)], option a. This matches my earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

Taking logarithms gives (4-x)\ln 3=(2x+3)\ln 8, hence x=(4\ln 3-3\ln 8)/(\ln 3+2\ln 8). This matches my earlier answer and the submitted response graded Correct. Math Academy's worked solution differs only in logarithm notation and parentheses.

Taking base-2 logarithms gives x+1=x\log_2(3), so x=1/(\log_2(3)-1). Math Academy states the same result: x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{2}⁡(3)-1}. The mathematics and worked solution agree. No learner grade or answer fields are supplied; the previously returned field named x was unsupported and is removed.

Taking natural logarithms gives x+1=x\ln 2+\ln 5, hence x=(\ln 5-1)/(1-\ln 2). This agrees with Math Academy's concluding result: x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}. No learner grade or answer fields are supplied.

Taking logarithms gives (x+2)\ln 5=(x-2)\ln 9, hence x=2(\ln 5+\ln 9)/(\ln 9-\ln 5). This agrees with Math Academy's concluding result: x & =\frac{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9))}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}. All displayed algebraic steps are valid. question.name: Question 1
question.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x-2} & ={5}^{4x} \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x-2}) & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
x-2={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{4x}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x-2=4x{log}_{3}⁡(5)
$$

Then, we solve for $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x & =2+4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-4x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =2 \\ x(1-4{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-4{log}_{3}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(5)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}≈1.464\,974.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2}{1-4(1.464\,974)}≈-0.412,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Question 1

Given that 3x−2=54x, what is the value of x? Round your answer to 3 decimal places.
x≈
−0.412

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take log3 on both sides of the equation:

3x−2=54xlog3⁡(3x−2)=log3⁡(54x)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side:

x−2=log3⁡(54x).

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−2=4xlog3⁡(5)

Then, we solve for x, as follows: x−2=4xlog3⁡(5)x=2+4xlog3⁡(5)x−4xlog3⁡(5)=2x(1−4log3⁡(5))=2x=21−4log3⁡(5)

Using the change of base formula, we have log3⁡(5)=ln⁡(5)ln⁡(3)≈1.464974.

Finally, we can approximate x as x≈21−4(1.464974)≈−0.412, rounded to 3 decimal places.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that ${3}^{x}={2}^{x-1},$ what is the value of $x?$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x} & ={2}^{x-1} \\ {log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x}) & ={log}_{3}⁡({2}^{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡({2}^{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(x-1){log}_{3}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(x-1){log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x & =x{log}_{3}⁡(2)-{log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(2) & =-{log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(2)) & =-{log}_{3}⁡(2) \\ x & =-\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(2)}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(2)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}≈0.630\,930.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈-\frac{0.630\,930}{1-0.630\,930}≈-1.710,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$

$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{3}⁡(2)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}≈0.630\,930.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈-\frac{0.630\,930}{1-0.630\,930}≈-1.710,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x-5}={4}^{x}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-5} & ={4}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & =5 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-5} & ={4}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & =5 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex−5=4x?

a
5(1−ln⁡4)
b
51−ln⁡4
c
5ln⁡4
d
1+ln⁡45
e
ln⁡5−ln⁡4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−5=4xln⁡(ex−5)=ln⁡(4x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x−5=ln⁡(4x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−5=xln⁡4

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x−5=xln⁡4x−xln⁡4=5x(1−ln⁡4)=5x=51−ln⁡4

Question 3
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex−5=4x?

a
5(1−ln⁡4)
b
51−ln⁡4
c
5ln⁡4
d
1+ln⁡45
e
ln⁡5−ln⁡4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−5=4xln⁡(ex−5)=ln⁡(4x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x−5=ln⁡(4x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−5=xln⁡4

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x−5=xln⁡4x−xln⁡4=5x(1−ln⁡4)=5x=51−ln⁡4

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x-1}={3}^{x}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-1} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex−1=3x?

a
1−ln⁡3
b
11−ln⁡3
c
1−ln⁡33
d
ln⁡2−ln⁡3
e
log⁡31+ln⁡3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−1=3xln⁡(ex−1)=ln⁡(3x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x−1=ln⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−1=xln⁡3

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x−1=xln⁡3x−xln⁡3=1x(1−ln⁡3)=1x=11−ln⁡3

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-1} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex−1=3x?

a
1−ln⁡3
b
11−ln⁡3
c
1−ln⁡33
d
ln⁡2−ln⁡3
e
log⁡31+ln⁡3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−1=3xln⁡(ex−1)=ln⁡(3x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x−1=ln⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−1=xln⁡3

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x−1=xln⁡3x−xln⁡3=1x(1−ln⁡3)=1x=11−ln⁡3

Question 4
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex−1=3x?

a
1−ln⁡3
b
11−ln⁡3
c
1−ln⁡33
d
ln⁡2−ln⁡3
e
log⁡31+ln⁡3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex−1=3xln⁡(ex−1)=ln⁡(3x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x−1=ln⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x−1=xln⁡3

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x−1=xln⁡3x−xln⁡3=1x(1−ln⁡3)=1x=11−ln⁡3

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & ={2}^{x+3} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x+3}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+2=(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x+2 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2 \\ x & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{x+4}={6}^{2-3x}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+4} & ={6}^{2-3x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2-3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Find the solution of 3x+4=62−3x.

a
2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)
b
12ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)
c
2ln⁡(6)−ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+ln⁡(6)
d
1ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)
e
2ln⁡(6)−2ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+ln⁡(6)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

3x+4=62−3xln⁡(3x+4)=ln⁡(62−3x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+4)ln⁡(3)=(2−3x)ln⁡(6)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+4)ln⁡(3)=(2−3x)ln⁡(6)xln⁡(3)+4ln⁡(3)=2ln⁡(6)−3xln⁡(6)xln⁡(3)+3xln⁡(6)=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)x(ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6))=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)x=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+4} & ={6}^{2-3x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2-3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Find the solution of 3x+4=62−3x.

a
2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)
b
12ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)
c
2ln⁡(6)−ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+ln⁡(6)
d
1ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)
e
2ln⁡(6)−2ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+ln⁡(6)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

3x+4=62−3xln⁡(3x+4)=ln⁡(62−3x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+4)ln⁡(3)=(2−3x)ln⁡(6)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+4)ln⁡(3)=(2−3x)ln⁡(6)xln⁡(3)+4ln⁡(3)=2ln⁡(6)−3xln⁡(6)xln⁡(3)+3xln⁡(6)=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)x(ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6))=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)x=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)
question.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases

solution.reasoning: Taking natural logarithms gives (x+4)\ln 3=(2-3x)\ln 6. Collecting terms yields x(\ln 3+3\ln 6)=2\ln 6-4\ln 3, so option a is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different equation.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{x+4}={6}^{2-3x}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+4} & ={6}^{2-3x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2-3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

3x+4=62−3xln⁡(3x+4)=ln⁡(62−3x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+4)ln⁡(3)=(2−3x)ln⁡(6)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+4)ln⁡(3)=(2−3x)ln⁡(6)xln⁡(3)+4ln⁡(3)=2ln⁡(6)−3xln⁡(6)xln⁡(3)+3xln⁡(6)=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)x(ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6))=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)x=2ln⁡(6)−4ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+3ln⁡(6)
